Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: New-onset dry, red, itchy rash on arms and hands noticed a few days ago after swimming in a chlorinated pool.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began shortly after swim; persistent over several days; coconut butter has not relieved symptoms.
- ENT symptoms: Patient denies throat swelling/closing sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, lip/tongue/uvular/facial swelling, ear pain/hearing changes, neck pain/swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: No prior skin problems; first episode. No previous ED visits or injections. Has tried coconut butter only.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies: Possible lactose intolerance (self-reported). No documented drug or environmental allergies.  
  • Medications: Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive pill) – dose/route/frequency not documented.
  • Rescue meds/device: None.
- Any relevant social context: Lives alone; primary-school teacher; high work-related stress recently.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Patient reports dry, red, itchy rash limited to arms and hands; no mention of vesicles, oozing, or systemic involvement.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor or respiratory distress reported.
- Mental status/associated features: Feels tired but otherwise well; no dizziness or syncope.
- Vitals/exam: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person: Patient is alone during call.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Likely irritant contact dermatitis secondary to chlorine exposure from recent swimming.
  Evidence: Acute onset post-swim, localized to exposed areas, red/dry/itchy without systemic features.
- DDx (consistent with transcript):
  1. Irritant contact dermatitis – high likelihood; explanation above.
  2. Atopic dermatitis – medium likelihood; family history of atopy and recent stress, but no personal history and clear temporal link to swim.
  3. Allergic contact dermatitis – medium likelihood; immune-mediated reaction to chlorine or pool chemicals possible; absence of vesicles noted.
  Opposing evidence for each listed in DDx (see reasoning); no conflicts with transcript.

Plan:
- Immediate/ongoing management:
  • Prescribe mild-to-moderate potency topical corticosteroid for affected areas (per clinician discussion).  
  • Start regular emollient (non-scented) multiple times daily.  
  • OTC non-sedating antihistamine (e.g., loratadine) for pruritus.  
- Patient instructions:
  • Avoid swimming and minimize exposure to pool chemicals/harsh soaps until rash resolves.  
  • Apply emollient generously; use lukewarm water for washing; avoid scratching.  
  • Monitor for spreading rash, cracking/oozing skin, signs of infection (pain, pus), or any new systemic/airway symptoms (breathing difficulty, facial or tongue swelling); seek urgent care if these occur.  
- Follow-up:
  • Review in one week if no improvement or sooner if worsening.  
  • Consider dermatology or allergy referral if recurrent or unclear.  

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: Exact steroid prescribed (name/potency), dosage/frequency for Microgynon, complete allergy list (foods/drugs/environmentals), documentation of vitals and physical exam findings, auto-injector history (not relevant but usually checked in allergy assessment).  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional minor incompleteness (patient’s short responses) but overall sufficient for clinical documentation.
